title: The Suez Canal: why it is strategic
subtitle: 1869 to today
subject: comprendreLeMonde
description: A 193-kilometer water corridor carries 12% of world trade. One ship ran aground in 2021 and stalled the planet: welcome to **Suez**.

hero.hook: 193 kilometers of canal, 12% of world trade: this is the story of the most strategic passage on earth.

blocks.text: The **Suez Canal**, in Egypt, is one of the most strategic crossing points on the planet. By linking the Mediterranean to the Red Sea, it spares ships the long trip around Africa by the **Cape of Good Hope**, cutting nearly 7,000 kilometers off the route between Europe and Asia.

Beyond its economic role, the canal is a reliable barometer of world power. From its colonial construction to its nationalization by Egypt in 1956, and on to the maritime tensions of today, it remains a major question of sovereignty.

sections.title: The colonial era: a bridge to empire

blocks.text: The cut through the Isthmus of Suez was led by the French engineer Ferdinand de Lesseps. Between 1859 and 1869, thousands of Egyptian laborers dug this 193-kilometer waterway.

blocks.caption: The opening of the Suez Canal in November 1869 crowned a decade of enormous works

blocks.text: When it opened in 1869, the canal was run by a private company funded mostly with French money. Britain was skeptical at first, but quickly saw how important the route was for its colonies. Taking advantage of the huge debts of the khedive, the ruler of Egypt, it bought his shares in 1875 and became the main shareholder.
For the opening in 1869, the composer Giuseppe Verdi was asked to write an opera for the occasion. That is how the famous *Aida* was born.

This foreign control created growing tension. For most of the 20th century, Egyptian nationalists saw the canal as the symbol of a colonial humiliation, a British enclave in the heart of a country seeking its independence.

The year 1956 marked a historic break. The Egyptian president Gamal Abdel Nasser, a leading figure of **[[Pan-Arabism]]**, nationalized the canal company on July 26, 1956. His aim was to use the canal's revenue to pay for a great dam on the Nile that the Western powers had just refused to finance.

The reaction was immediate. France and the United Kingdom, which had just lost their stake, joined Israel in a secret military offensive. The canal was occupied, but the operation enraged American president Eisenhower, who had not been told and feared the attack would push the developing world toward the USSR.

Under American pressure, the European powers were forced into a humiliating withdrawal. It was the end of France and the United Kingdom as front-rank colonial powers, and the triumph of Nasser, now an idol across the Arab world. The episode is still known as **[[The Suez Crisis (1956)]]**.

sections.title: A vital artery under modern strain

blocks.text: Today the Suez Canal is still the lungs of world shipping: about 12% of global trade and nearly 20,000 vessels pass through it every year. But its narrowness, next to the sheer size of modern ships, is a major weakness.

On March 26, 2021, the giant container ship **[[Ever Given]]** ran aground across the canal and blocked all traffic for six days. The blockage backed up more than 400 ships and cost the world economy around 400 million dollars an hour.

blocks.caption: In March 2021, the container ship Ever Given blocked the Suez Canal for six days

blocks.text: Technical accidents are not the only danger: regional politics threatens that stability too. Between 2023 and 2024, missile attacks launched by the **[[Houthis]]** from Yemen against commercial shipping pushed many owners to reroute their fleets around southern Africa, a three-week detour that drives costs sharply higher.
To stay competitive, Egypt launched the “new Suez Canal” in 2015, doubling capacity along some stretches. The canal is also becoming an economic zone that attracts Chinese and European investment.

Canal revenue is still one of Egypt's main sources of foreign currency, which makes the country extremely watchful over the security of the **Bab-el-Mandeb** strait, the real southern gateway to the whole Suez system.

The Suez Canal, opened in 1869, went from a tool of British imperial control to a symbol of Egyptian sovereignty after the crisis of 1956. Today it carries 12% of world trade, but it stays vulnerable to technical accidents and to tension in the Red Sea.
